passage:
12 November
Irfan forgot my birthday. Completely. No call, no message, nothing, and then he posted photos from a cricket match that evening. My first thought at 11 p.m. was: he never really cared. Classic Irfan, always about himself.
Then I made myself write the other list. Irfan drove three hours to help me move flats in the rain. He sat with me in the hospital when Papa had his operation. He lent me money without asking when I'd pay it back.
Both lists are true. He's caring and he's careless. Those aren't opposites; they're just two facts about one person. I don't have to erase the first list because of the second.
So tomorrow I'll call and tell him it stung. Not a verdict on our whole friendship, just one thing that hurt.
Abhinav

qa.q: What did Irfan post on the evening of the birthday?
qa.a: Photos from a cricket match.

qa.q: Why did 'he never really cared' feel true to Abhinav at 11 p.m.?
qa.a: The hurt of being forgotten was fresh and strong, so for that moment one careless act seemed to define the whole friendship.

qa.q: Which choice helped Abhinav keep the friendship steady?
qa.a: Writing the second list of Irfan's kindnesses and deciding to call about one thing that stung, instead of judging the whole friendship.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel when Abhinav calls tomorrow?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and sorry about forgetting, and relieved that Abhinav raised it as one hurt rather than ending things.

grounding: An adult hurt by a friend's forgotten birthday reminds themselves that the friend is both caring and careless, and plans a calm conversation instead of a verdict.

passage:
In the kasba of Nabha, Kiran and Salma ran a small tailoring shop together above the sweet shop. On Monday morning Kiran found the door unlocked and two bolts of wedding silk gone. Salma had forgotten to lock up again.
Kiran's first thought, standing in the empty doorway, was hot and total: she's useless, she's always been careless, I should never have trusted her. Then she sat on the step and made herself remember. Salma had sat up three nights with Kiran's baby during the fever. Salma had taught her to cut blouse patterns for nothing. Salma was kind, and Salma was careless. Both.
When Salma arrived, pale, Kiran said, "I'm very angry about the silk. I'm not angry about you. From now on, I lock up." Salma cried, and then they walked to the police station together.

qa.q: What was missing from the shop on Monday morning?
qa.a: Two bolts of wedding silk.

qa.q: Why did 'she's useless' feel so true to Kiran in the doorway?
qa.a: The loss was sudden and costly, so her anger made one careless act feel like the whole truth about Salma.

qa.q: Which choice helped Kiran respond without breaking the partnership?
qa.a: Remembering Salma's kindness on the step, then separating her anger about the silk from her view of Salma, and taking over the locking up herself.

qa.q: What might Salma have feared as she arrived at the shop?
qa.a: That Kiran would end their partnership or friendship; hearing 'I'm not angry about you' likely brought huge relief along with guilt.

grounding: A woman whose business partner's carelessness cost them stock reminds herself the partner is also deeply kind, and responds without an explosion.

passage:
Diary, Saturday
I got my hair cut short like the captain of our women's team. Everyone at the nets says I look like a boy. I don't care. I'm the only girl there anyway. I practised her stance for one hour in the garage: bat up high, chin down, eyes still. I even did her little double tap of the bat before each ball. At the nets I hit three fours in a row!! I felt STRONG.
But then I copied the other thing she does, pointing the bat at the bowler after a four. Minakshi was bowling and she stopped smiling. Coach said, "Hit hard. No pointing." I felt silly.
Tomorrow: same stance, no pointing. The captain always shakes hands after matches too. I'll copy that.
Sharmila

qa.q: How many fours did Sharmila hit in a row at the nets?
qa.a: Three fours in a row.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila feel 'STRONG' when she used the captain's stance?
qa.a: Copying her hero made her feel some of the captain's power and confidence, and hitting fours seemed to prove it. 😊

qa.q: What choice did Sharmila make about which habits to copy, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Keeping the stance and the handshakes but dropping the pointing, because the handshake shows respect while the pointing only upset Minakshi.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when Sharmila pointed the bat at her?
qa.a: Minakshi probably felt mocked or shown up, which is why she stopped smiling.

grounding: A girl copies her cricket hero's haircut, stance and gestures, feels stronger, and learns the swagger doesn't come with the skill.

passage:
Nine-year-old Indu, in her village outside Karnal, had pinned up a newspaper photo of the district's gold-medal sprinter, a young woman who had grown up three villages away. Indu now tied her hair in the same high knot, wore a sweatband on one wrist, and started every morning with the warm-up she had seen on the TV at the tea stall. She even walked like her, shoulders back. "Early to bed, early to track," she told her little sister Payal, in the sprinter's firm voice.
But when Payal beat her in a race to the well, Indu snapped, "Champions don't lose to babies," and stalked off. Payal's lip wobbled. That evening Indu came back with a guava. "Champions also say sorry," she mumbled.

qa.q: What did Indu wear on one wrist?
qa.a: A sweatband.

qa.q: Why did Indu snap 'Champions don't lose to babies' at Payal?
qa.a: Losing hurt her new champion image, and she borrowed a proud, swaggering attitude to cover the embarrassment.

qa.q: What turning point shows Indu choosing the better part of her hero?
qa.a: Coming back with a guava and saying 'Champions also say sorry', which keeps the discipline and drops the swagger.

qa.q: How might Payal feel about her sister's new champion act?
qa.a: Admiring at first, then hurt when the swagger turned on her; the apology probably made her feel close again.

grounding: A village girl copies a local sprinting champion's style and voice, feels stronger, and briefly borrows the swagger too.

passage:
At his Saturday cricket club in south London, eleven-year-old Jin had started copying his favourite batter from the television: the same blond streak in his fringe (his mum had allowed one), the same wide stance, the same slow walk to the crease. With the stance, his drives actually got better. He felt taller walking out. Chidi, who opened the batting with him, said, "You look like a proper pro."
But Jin also started copying the batter's hard stare at bowlers and the muttering at umpires. When the club umpire gave him out leg before wicket, Jin threw his bat down. Coach took him aside. "Your hero hits beautifully. Copy that. And copy how he apologises afterwards, too." Jin went red and picked up his bat.

qa.q: What choice did Coach help Jin see?
qa.a: To keep copying the good batting and the apologies, but drop the stare and the bat-throwing swagger.

qa.q: How might the club umpire have felt when Jin threw his bat?
qa.a: Disrespected and uncomfortable, since a young player was treating a fair decision as an insult.

grounding: A boy in London copies a cricket hero's look and stance, feels stronger, and also picks up the hero's swagger.

passage:
Didi, you asked about my warning letter. You know how in Class 8 those guys used to hide my bag and call me "Hemu the Hippo", every day? And there's this new kid, Omkar: small, thick glasses, stammers when he reads. Last week one of them laughed at him and I... joined in. Then I started it myself. I called him "Owl". I pushed his books off the desk. Everyone laughed with me, not at me. It felt safe? Like I'd climbed out of the hole. Yesterday I saw Omkar eating lunch alone behind the water tank, the same place I used to hide. And I felt sick. Your little brother Hemant is doing to him exactly what they did to me. I don't know how to stop without looking weak.
Didi sat close and listened. "What they did to you was never your fault. Tonight we tell Mummy; tomorrow, your class teacher, about Omkar too."

qa.q: What did Hemant start calling Omkar?
qa.a: "Owl".

qa.q: Why did mocking Omkar feel 'safe' to Hemant?
qa.a: After years as the target, being on the laughing side felt like climbing out of the hole; the powerful role seemed to protect him from being picked on again.

qa.q: What could Hemant do next to stop without 'looking weak'?
qa.a: Stop the name-calling, apologise to Omkar privately, and, as Didi planned, tell Mummy tonight and the class teacher tomorrow about both what happened to him and what he did; stopping takes more strength than joining in.

qa.q: What is it like for Omkar to eat lunch alone behind the water tank?
qa.a: Probably lonely and frightening, the same hiding place and pain Hemant once knew.

grounding: A teenager who was bullied for years tells his sister he has started mocking a weaker boy because the powerful role feels safer, sees he is repeating the harm, and his sister responds that same day.

passage:
I'm Saurabh, and I've been in Chetan's section since Class 6. Back then the older boys made Chetan do their homework and flicked his ears on the bus. He never told anyone, as far as I know. This year he's in Class 10 and taller than most of us, and something's changed. Now he's the one on the bus making a Class 7 boy, Nikhil, sit on the floor. Yesterday he grabbed Nikhil's tiffin and passed it around. Some people laughed. I didn't know what to do.
I can't tell what's going on in Chetan's head. But I saw him look out of the window afterwards, jaw tight, the way he used to when it was him on the floor.
Today I told our class teacher what I'd seen on the bus. She said she would speak to both of them, and the bus in-charge, this afternoon.

qa.q: What did Chetan grab from Nikhil yesterday?
qa.a: Nikhil's tiffin, which Chetan passed around.

qa.q: What might Chetan's tight jaw at the window suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Perhaps a flash of old hurt or guilt, seeing Nikhil where he used to be, even while he played the powerful role.

qa.q: Which choice of Saurabh's was the right one, and why?
qa.a: Telling the class teacher what happened on the bus, because Nikhil needed protecting and Chetan needed an adult to step in; the teacher acted that same afternoon.

qa.q: How might Nikhil experience the bus rides now?
qa.a: He likely dreads them, feeling humiliated and helpless on the floor, much as Chetan once did.

grounding: A classmate sees a boy who was once tormented now humiliating a younger student, and reports it to a teacher who acts the same day.

September. At his new school, Pankaj kept his head down. At his old one he had been shoved into lockers as "the fat boy" for two years. He still flinched when anyone raised a hand near him.
November. Pankaj had made friends, loud ones. In the canteen, one of them pointed at Dinesh, a small Class 8 boy who carried a violin case, and Pankaj called out, "Oi, Fiddler!" The table roared. Pankaj felt warm, part of something. The next day he said it again, louder.
December. Uma Ma'am, the class teacher, called Pankaj in after she found Dinesh crying by the stairs. "Dinesh told me what's been said," she said. Pankaj stared at the floor. "I know what that felt like," he whispered. "I'm doing it anyway." Uma Ma'am nodded. "Then let's work out how you stop, and how you put it right with Dinesh. Both your families will hear from me today."

qa.q: What had Pankaj been called at his old school?
qa.a: "The fat boy".

qa.q: Why did mocking Dinesh make Pankaj feel 'warm, part of something'?
qa.a: After two years as the target, being on the laughing side made him feel safe and accepted among loud friends.

qa.q: What choice did Uma Ma'am make, and why is it the right response?
qa.a: She acted the same day, listening to Pankaj without excusing him, planning how he stops and makes it right with Dinesh, and telling both families.

qa.q: What was it like for Dinesh to be called 'Fiddler' in the canteen?
qa.a: Humiliating and frightening, bad enough that he ended up crying by the stairs.

Three months into her traineeship at the newspaper office, Aditi noticed she had started saying "Let's not bury the lede" in every meeting. It was Ishita's line, the senior editor's, along with "Tighten it, then tighten it again" and a habit of tapping a pen twice before disagreeing. Aditi had caught herself tapping too. And it worked: when she used Ishita's phrases, the other trainees listened, and her own voice sounded steadier.
On Friday, though, she pitched a story about her neighbourhood's water-tanker queue and heard herself say "Tighten it, then tighten it again" about a piece that actually needed room to breathe. She stopped. That evening she drew two columns in her notebook: "Ishita's that fit me" and "Ishita's that don't". The pen-tap went in the second.

qa.q: Which of Ishita's lines did Aditi say in every meeting?
qa.a: "Let's not bury the lede."

qa.q: Why does using Ishita's phrases make Aditi feel more confident?
qa.a: Borrowing an admired editor's words makes her voice sound steadier and gets the other trainees listening, like wearing a little of Ishita's authority.

qa.q: What turning point shows Aditi testing what genuinely fits her?
qa.a: Noticing on Friday that 'tighten it' didn't suit a story that needed room, then sorting Ishita's habits into two columns in her notebook.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel hearing a trainee repeat 'Let's not bury the lede'?
qa.a: Ishita might be amused and flattered, and curious to hear Aditi's own voice emerge.

grounding: A trainee journalist absorbs a senior editor's phrases and habits, feels more confident, and then begins sorting which ones truly fit her.

Dear Jasleen Ma'am,
It's been a year since I finished my apprenticeship in your carpentry workshop, and I have a confession. For my first six months at the new job, I talked exactly like you. "Measure twice, cut once, beta." "The wood tells you where it wants to split." I even called my apprentice "beta", and he's older than me! Your phrases made me feel like I knew what I was doing when I didn't yet.
Lately I've noticed some of them don't sound like me. I don't say "beta". I explain things with drawings, not proverbs. But "measure twice" stays forever. It's the best advice anyone ever gave me.
So thank you for lending me your voice until I found mine.
With respect,
Alka

qa.q: Which piece of advice does Alka say will stay forever?
qa.a: "Measure twice."

qa.q: Why did talking like Jasleen Ma'am make Alka feel capable in the first months?
qa.a: Using the mentor's phrases felt like carrying some of Jasleen Ma'am's skill and authority, which covered Alka's own uncertainty.

qa.q: What choice has Alka made about the borrowed phrases, and why is it healthy?
qa.a: Keeping 'measure twice' but dropping 'beta' and the proverbs in favour of drawings, so Alka holds on to what fits and grows a personal style.

qa.q: How might Jasleen Ma'am feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Probably proud and moved, seeing her teaching carried on while Alka finds a voice that fits. 🙂

grounding: A former apprentice writes to a mentor about having copied her phrases to feel confident, and then keeping only the ones that truly fit.

So when I joined the sales team, I basically became Darshan. He was the senior who closed every deal, and I copied everything: "Let's park that thought," "Help me understand your pain point," even the way he leaned back with his hands behind his head. And honestly, it helped. I was twenty-one and terrified of clients, and borrowing his lines felt like borrowing armour. By month four I was closing deals.
Then one client, an older aunty who ran a tailoring unit, said, "Beta, why are you talking like a textbook?" I laughed, but it stung. That night I went through my lines one by one. "Help me understand" fits me. Leaning back doesn't; I'm a leaner-forward. "Park that thought" I dropped. Now I sound like Urmila, with a bit of Darshan mixed in.

qa.a: "Beta, why are you talking like a textbook?"

qa.q: What turning point pushed Urmila to test which habits fit?
qa.a: The client's textbook comment, after which Urmila went through the lines one by one and kept only those that felt natural.

In the small garage in Toronto where he repaired bicycles, Omar heard himself say it: "If you can't do it properly, don't do it at all." Ivan, his new apprentice, froze with the spanner in hand. It was his father's sentence, word for word, in his father's sharp tone. Omar remembered being twelve, redoing a school project at midnight while his father stood over him.
His father had also taught him to check every bolt twice and never leave a job half-done, and that was why customers trusted Omar's shop. That evening, locking up, Omar decided: the bolts stay; the tone goes.
The next morning he showed Ivan how to true a wheel, slowly. When Ivan got it wrong, Omar said, "Close. Try again, I'll watch."

qa.q: What sentence did Omar hear himself say?

qa.q: What did Omar feel when he recognised his father's sentence?

qa.q: How might Ivan experience the change from the first day to the next morning?

In her second week teaching Class 5 at the municipal school, Ritu heard her own voice across the classroom: "Zubin! Is this handwriting or chicken scratch? Do it again." The room went silent. Zubin's ears turned red. Ritu felt a cold drop in her stomach. That was Papa, exactly. Papa, who checked her homework every night with a red pen and a raised eyebrow. Papa, who also taught her to finish every task and never skip a line of working, which was why she had topped her teaching course.
In the staff room at lunch she wrote on a sticky note: KEEP: high standards, finish the work. DROP: the sarcasm.
After lunch she knelt by Zubin's desk. "Your letters are rushing. Let's slow down the g's together." Zubin wrote three careful g's and looked up, hopeful.

qa.q: What did Ritu write under DROP on her sticky note?
qa.a: The sarcasm.

qa.q: Which choice turned an inherited pattern into a deliberate one?
qa.a: Writing KEEP and DROP lists at lunch, then kneeling to help Zubin slow down, keeping high standards without the sarcasm.

Dear Dilnaz,
You laughed on the phone when I told you I'd said "Time is money, not a toy" to my new flatmate. But afterwards I couldn't sleep. That's Abbu's line. I say it in his voice, with his frown. He said it to us every time we were five minutes late.

Class 3 teacher's note, Thursday
On Wednesday at recess, Shankar called Lokesh "stupid" in front of the others when Lokesh dropped the ball. Lokesh sat alone for the rest of recess.
This morning Shankar came in early and slipped a shiny tiger sticker onto Lokesh's desk without a word. He hovered nearby, watching. Lokesh looked at the sticker, then at Shankar, and didn't smile.
At lunch I sat with Shankar. I told him the sticker was a kind idea and asked what it was for. He mumbled, "For yesterday." I asked what Lokesh might need to hear. After a long pause he said, "Sorry?" He went and said it. Lokesh stuck the tiger on his pencil box. They played together at afternoon recess.

qa.q: What did Shankar put on Lokesh's desk?
qa.a: A shiny tiger sticker.

qa.q: Why did Shankar give the sticker without saying anything?
qa.a: He felt guilty about calling Lokesh stupid and hoped the gift would cancel it without the harder step of saying sorry.

qa.q: Which choice of the teacher's helped finish the repair?
qa.a: Praising the sticker idea, then asking what Lokesh might need to hear, so Shankar found the word 'sorry' himself.

qa.q: Why didn't Lokesh smile at the sticker at first?
qa.a: The hurt of being called stupid in front of others was still there, and a silent sticker didn't show that Shankar understood what he'd done.

grounding: A teacher notes how a boy tries to cancel an insult with a silent sticker, and helps him add the apology that finishes the repair.

passage:

Today I did a weird thing. Yesterday I told Ganga her drawing looked like a baby did it. She had spent the whole art period on it. She went quiet and put it in her bag.
So this morning I gave her my best pencil, the one with the eraser shaped like a mango. I didn't say why. She said thanks, but she didn't look at me properly. All day I felt like I had a stone in my stomach.

Chandrika had called Amandeep "kanjoos" in front of the whole line at their village school near Hoshiarpur, just because Amandeep wouldn't share her pickle at lunch. Everyone laughed. Amandeep's face went hot.
The next morning Chandrika walked the long way past the sugarcane fields and picked three ripe ber from her Nani's tree. At school she dropped them into Amandeep's lap without a word and ran to her seat. Amandeep held the ber in her palm, not eating.
At recess she came over. "Is this for yesterday?" Chandrika nodded, looking at her slippers. "Then say it," Amandeep said, not unkindly. Chandrika took a breath. "Sorry for calling you kanjoos. It was mean." Amandeep popped a ber into her mouth. "Okay. They're sour, though."

qa.a: Three ripe ber from her Nani's tree.

qa.a: She felt guilty and embarrassed, hoping the gift would cancel the insult without having to face Amandeep and talk about it.

qa.q: What turning point completed the repair between the girls?
qa.a: Amandeep asking 'Then say it', and Chandrika actually apologising, which turned the silent gift into a real repair.

qa.q: Why might Amandeep have held the ber without eating at first?
qa.a: She was still hurt from being laughed at and needed to know the gift meant sorry before she could accept it.

grounding: A village girl tries to undo a mean name with a silent gift of fruit, and her friend asks for the apology that finishes the repair.

Friday. Tanuja screamed at her father when he said no to the school trip. "You never trust me! You're the worst!" She slammed the door.
Saturday. Tanuja woke at six. She mopped every floor, washed the scooter, ironed Papa's office shirts and made him ginger tea. She placed it on the table and walked away before he could say anything. When her friend Zeenat called, Tanuja said, "I'm busy. Being a perfect daughter."
Sunday. Papa found her polishing the steel almirah for the second time. He sat on the bed. "Beta, the house has never been cleaner," he said gently. "But I've been waiting for something else." Tanuja's hands stopped. She stared at the cloth. "I'm sorry I called you the worst," she whispered. Papa nodded. "Thank you. Now sit. Let's talk about the trip."

In the kasba of Palanpur, Sudha had worked beside Tanvir at his family's cloth shop all summer before college reopened. On Tuesday, in front of two customers, he snapped, "Can't you do anything right? Even a child can fold a saree." She kept folding, cheeks burning.
On Thursday he walked in smiling and put a box on the counter: a new phone, far better than her cracked one. "For you. Hardworking people deserve good things."
Sudha looked at the box. It felt like he was trying to fold Tuesday away and put it on a high shelf. She pushed it gently back. "Tanvir, thank you, but I can't take this. What I'd like is for us to talk about what you said on Tuesday."
His smile slipped. "It was nothing."
"It wasn't nothing to me," she said.

qa.q: What did Tanvir say to Sudha on Tuesday?
qa.a: "Can't you do anything right? Even a child can fold a saree."

qa.q: Why did the new phone feel wrong to Sudha?
qa.a: It seemed like an attempt to put Tuesday's insult away without talking about it, so accepting it would feel like agreeing the hurt didn't matter.

qa.q: What choice did Sudha make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She returned the gift kindly and asked to talk about Tuesday, which keeps the relationship open while making clear that words matter more than presents. 👍

qa.q: What might Tanvir be feeling when his smile slips?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and uneasy, since the gift was his way to avoid admitting what he said, and now he has to face it.

grounding: A young woman insulted in front of customers is handed an expensive phone with a smile, and kindly says she would rather talk about what was said.

In their shared flat in Berlin, Felix had mocked Aiko's accent at a party, loudly, doing an impression while his friends laughed. Aiko left early.
The next evening Felix knocked on her door holding a bag from an expensive bookshop: a beautiful illustrated edition of the novel she had been saving up for. "Peace offering!" he said, with his brightest grin.
Aiko held the heavy book. It was exactly what she wanted, which somehow made it worse. It felt like the party was being wrapped in expensive paper and put away. "Felix," she said, "this is really generous. But I'd rather hear what you think about last night."
Felix shifted from foot to foot. "I mean, it was a joke..."
"It didn't feel like one," Aiko said. "Can we talk about it? The book can wait."

qa.a: An illustrated edition of the novel she had been saving up for.

qa.a: It felt as if the hurtful impression was being wrapped up and put away without being talked about, as though her hurt didn't need words.

qa.q: What choice did Aiko make, and why might it help?
qa.a: She thanked Felix but asked to talk about the party first, making clear in a kind way that the conversation mattered more than the book.

qa.a: He may feel guilty but awkward about admitting the impression was hurtful, and a gift felt easier than saying he was wrong.

grounding: A student in Berlin mocked at a party receives an expensive book as a 'peace offering' and gently says she would rather talk about what happened.

In March I missed the deadline for a client's tax filing at our accounts firm. It cost them a late fee, and it was my fault; I'd let it slide under other work. After that I stayed until ten every night for five weeks. I rechecked every file twice. When Lalit, my team lead, offered to split my load, I said "No, I've got it," too quickly. I skipped lunch, then weekends. I think I was trying to pay it off, like a fine, with my evenings.
In week six I fell asleep at my desk and woke with the keyboard printed on my cheek. Lalit sat me down. "Chaitanya, you made one mistake. You told the client. We fixed the process. It's done. Working yourself sick doesn't make it more done."
I cried a little, embarrassingly. Then I went home at six.

qa.a: Five weeks.

qa.a: Chaitanya felt the mistake had to be paid off personally, like a fine, and accepting help would have felt like not suffering enough for it.

qa.q: What turning point helped Chaitanya stop the penance?
qa.a: Falling asleep at the desk, and Lalit pointing out that the mistake was owned, told and fixed, so extra suffering added nothing.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt watching Chaitanya refuse help for weeks?
qa.a: Worried and a bit helpless, seeing a capable colleague wear down over something already settled.

grounding: An employee who missed a deadline works late for weeks and refuses help as penance, until a team lead points out the mistake is already owned and fixed.

Supervisor's note, 18 July
Mahima, one of our junior nurses, gave a patient's evening medicine late on 2 July. The patient was not harmed, it was reported properly, and we reviewed the handover process. It was a gap in the system as much as a personal one.
Since then Mahima has taken extra shifts every week, comes in early, stays late, and has refused every offer of help, including mine. Yesterday she was restocking supplies at 11 p.m. on her day off. She looks exhausted and has lost her usual laugh.
Today I spoke to her. I said the mistake was real, she owned it well, and the matter is closed. Extra shifts don't undo it; they only wear her down. We agreed: no extra shifts for a month, and a chat with the staff counsellor if the guilt keeps sitting heavy.
Sharmila Nair, Ward Supervisor

Another late night at the design studio. Third week in a row. Ever since I sent the client the wrong version of the brochure and they printed 500 copies, I've been trying to fix it by working harder than anyone.
